label: The Moral Argument
text: The Moral Argument for the existence of God argues that objective moral values and duties are real, and that God is the best explanation for their objective reality and binding force.

children.label: P1 — If God does not exist, objective moral values and duties do not exist
children.text: The first premise is not about whether atheists can behave morally. Belief in God is not required to act kindly, courageously, justly, or lovingly. The issue is whether atheism can ground objective moral values and duties. The argument claims that God's existence is required for moral values and duties to be objectively real and binding.

children.label: The issue is grounding, not moral behavior
children.text: People of many worldviews can recognize and practice moral behavior. The deeper question is whether, on atheism or naturalism, moral values and duties are anything more than evolved preferences, social conventions, or subjective attitudes.

children.label: Atheists can be moral people
children.text: Many atheists are kind, courageous, just, generous, and loving. Their moral lives can be admirable, so morality does not seem to require belief in God.

children.label: Moral behavior and moral ontology are different questions
children.text: This misunderstands the argument. The claim is not that atheists cannot be moral people. The claim is that if God does not exist, there is no adequate foundation for objective moral values and duties. How people behave and what makes moral values objectively real are different questions.

children.label: Euthyphro: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?
children.text: If something is good only because God commands it, morality seems arbitrary. If God commands something because it is already good, then goodness seems independent of God.

children.label: Goodness is grounded in God's nature
children.text: The dilemma overlooks a third option: goodness is grounded in God's own nature. God does not arbitrarily invent morality, nor does He conform to a standard outside Himself. His commands express His essentially good nature.

children.label: Objective morality can be grounded without God through atheistic moral Platonism
children.text: Atheistic moral Platonism holds that moral facts are abstract, necessary truths that exist independently of God, human opinion, and social convention.

children.label: Abstract moral facts do not explain personal obligation
children.text: Abstract moral facts do not seem able to impose personal obligations, generate moral responsibility, or explain why we are duty-bound to obey them. It would also be surprising, on atheism, if blind evolutionary processes produced creatures whose moral intuitions reliably track abstract moral truths.

children.label: Human flourishing can ground morality
children.text: Morality can be grounded in what promotes human flourishing. Actions are good when they help human beings thrive and wrong when they needlessly damage human life, cooperation, or well-being.

children.label: Flourishing still needs a moral foundation
children.text: Human flourishing may describe what humans naturally value, but it does not by itself explain why human flourishing is objectively good or morally obligatory. What grounds the special moral value of human beings if atheism is true? Privileging human flourishing over the flourishing of other species can appear arbitrary unless there is a deeper grounding for human dignity and moral worth.

children.label: P2 — Objective moral values and duties do exist
children.text: Our moral experience gives us reason to believe that some things are truly evil, not merely personally disliked or socially disapproved. Torturing children for fun, genocide, betrayal, cruelty, and injustice seem objectively wrong. Likewise, love, justice, mercy, courage, and compassion seem genuinely good.

children.label: Moral experience supports objective moral reality
children.text: Our basic moral experience gives us prima facie reason to believe that some actions are objectively right or wrong. We should not reject this unless we have a strong defeater.

children.label: Moral beliefs vary across cultures
children.text: Cultures often disagree about moral rules, priorities, and practices. This variation may suggest that moral beliefs are social constructions rather than perceptions of objective moral facts.

children.label: Disagreement does not disprove moral facts
children.text: Moral disagreement does not prove there are no moral facts, just as scientific disagreement does not prove there are no scientific facts. Cultures may perceive moral truths imperfectly. There is also significant cross-cultural agreement on many core moral norms.

children.label: Sociobiology explains our moral intuitions
children.text: Our sense of right and wrong may have developed because it helped our ancestors survive, cooperate, and pass on their genes. Moral intuition may therefore be a product of evolution rather than awareness of objective moral truth.

children.label: Sociobiology does not address the truth of moral values and duties
children.text: Sociobiology may explain how human beings came to have moral beliefs, but it does not show whether those beliefs are true or false. The origin of a belief is not the same thing as its truth. If God exists, He could use evolutionary processes as part of the means by which human beings become aware of real moral values and duties. Therefore, sociobiology does not, by itself, show that moral values and duties are illusory.

children.label: Sociobiology does not defeat moral justification without assuming atheism
children.text: The sociobiological objection often tries to remove our justification for believing in objective moral values and duties. But to do that, it must assume atheism or naturalism is already true, so that moral beliefs are merely survival-oriented byproducts rather than awareness of real moral truths. That assumption is being smuggled in rather than argued for. If our cognitive faculties are aimed only at survival and not truth, this concern can spread beyond morality and undermine confidence in all our beliefs, including atheism, naturalism, and the sociobiological explanation itself. Survival value does not guarantee true belief.

children.label: ∴ God exists as the ground of objective moral reality
children.text: If objective moral values and duties exist, and if they require a personal, morally perfect ground, then the best explanation is God. God's nature is the standard of goodness, and God's commands express moral duties.

children.label: God's nature is the moral standard
children.text: The conclusion does not depend on morality being created by arbitrary divine will. It appeals to God's essentially good nature as the standard of goodness, with divine commands expressing the duties that flow from that nature.
